response:
# Plan: triage agent, SPE round r01

I made three assumptions to fill gaps in the request:
- The 40 tickets will arrive as one CSV export. Each row holds the ticket text and the support lead's category and priority.
- The agent will be written in Python with the Anthropic SDK.
- Model IDs will be pinned at build time from the current Claude docs. They will not come from memory.

## 1. Specify

### Requirements (r01)

| ID | Requirement | Source | Test |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Give each ticket exactly one category: billing, bug, how-to, account, or outage. | User: "assigns a category (billing, bug, how-to, account, outage)" | Schema check, then category accuracy against the reference labels |
| R2 | Give each ticket exactly one priority from P1 to P4. | User: "a priority (P1 to P4)" | Schema check, priority exact match, priority within one level |
| R3 | Draft a first reply to the customer. | User: "drafts a first reply" | Code checks on the reply, then a judge rubric |
| R4 | Triage correctly. Target is category accuracy of at least 0.90 and priority within one level of at least 0.90. | User: "triage tickets correctly". Thresholds are default D2. | Category accuracy, priority within one |
| R5 | Never miss a P1 ticket. Target P1 recall is 1.00. | Default D2 | P1 recall |
| R6 | Triage cheaply. Report tokens and USD per ticket. Prefer the cheapest config whose category accuracy is within 0.03 of the best config. | User: "cheaply". Rule is default D1. | Token counts from API usage, USD from a pinned price table |
| R7 | Output is valid JSON every time. The fields are `category`, `priority`, `reply_draft`, and `rationale`. | Decision: downstream routing needs a fixed shape | JSON schema validation rate |
| R8 | The reply promises no refunds, credits, ETAs, or fixes. It contains no placeholders such as `[name]`. | Default D3 | Regex code checks, then the judge |
| R9 | The agent prompt never contains eval tickets or eval labels. | Decision: eval integrity | Hash scan of the prompt files against the eval set |

### Open decisions and logged defaults (`spe/spec/disagreements.md`)

| ID | Decision | Owner | Default used in r01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| D1 | What counts as "cheap" | User | No hard dollar cap. The R6 rule above applies. |
| D2 | What counts as "correct" | User | Category at least 0.90, priority within one at least 0.90, P1 recall 1.00 |
| D3 | How to grade replies with no reference replies | User, support lead | A code check plus an Opus judge rubric. The support lead reviews 10 graded drafts after the run to calibrate the judge. |
| D4 | Customer data in historical tickets | User | Store tickets and labels in `spe/evals/data/` and gitignore that folder. Commit only hashes and IDs. |
| D5 | Category and priority definitions | User, support lead | I draft written definitions from the five category names and a standard P1 to P4 policy. The support lead confirms them in round 2. The definitions are never tuned on the 40 eval tickets. |
| D6 | Model versions | Claude | Pin exact Sonnet, Haiku, and Opus IDs from the current docs during step 3. Record them in `spe/predictions/r01.yaml`. |

## 2. Predict

### Configs (each one changes one thing from A)

| Config | Model | Prompt |
|---|---|---|
| A (reference) | Sonnet, pinned | Zero-shot. System prompt holds the D5 definitions. |
| B | Sonnet, pinned | A plus 6 synthetic few-shot examples that I write. None of them comes from the eval set. |
| C | Haiku, pinned | Same as A |

### Predictions

A hit means the measured value falls inside the band. With 40 tickets, one ticket equals 0.025 of accuracy. That is why the bands are wide.

| Metric | A | B | C | Grader check | Why |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Schema-valid rate | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 1.00 ± 0.02 | 0.99 ± 0.02 | `jsonschema` validation of every trial output | Tool-use output with an enum schema forces the shape. |
| Category accuracy | 0.85 ± 0.07 | 0.88 ± 0.07 | 0.80 ± 0.08 | Exact match to the reference category, by majority vote over repeats | Billing and account overlap, and bug and outage overlap. Examples help at those boundaries. The smaller model is weaker there. |
| Priority exact match | 0.65 ± 0.10 | 0.70 ± 0.10 | 0.58 ± 0.10 | Exact match to the reference priority | Priority reflects the lead's judgment. My drafted policy will not match it fully. |
| Priority within one level | 0.92 ± 0.05 | 0.93 ± 0.05 | 0.88 ± 0.06 | Absolute difference of at most 1 | Most misses will be off by one level. |
| P1 recall | 0.90 ± 0.10 | 0.90 ± 0.10 | 0.80 ± 0.15 | Reference P1 tickets predicted as P1, divided by all reference P1 tickets | Outage language is explicit. The band is wide because few tickets are P1. |
| Reply pass rate | 0.85 ± 0.08 | 0.88 ± 0.08 | 0.78 ± 0.10 | First the R8 regex checks, then the judge rubric. All 4 rubric items must pass. | The no-promises rule is the most likely failure. |
| Label stability across 3 repeats | 0.95 ± 0.04 | 0.96 ± 0.04 | 0.92 ± 0.05 | Share of tickets where all 3 repeats agree on category and priority | Temperature 0 still varies a little. The smaller model varies more. |
| Mean input tokens per ticket | 1300 ± 300 | 2800 ± 500 | 1300 ± 300 | API `usage.input_tokens` | The definitions take about 800 tokens and a ticket about 400. The examples add about 1500. |
| Mean output tokens per ticket | 280 ± 80 | 280 ± 80 | 300 ± 100 | API `usage.output_tokens` | Most of the output is the reply draft. |

USD per ticket is computed from the token counts and the pinned price table. It is reported but not predicted. `same_as_last_round` is null because this is the first round.

## 3. Evaluate

### Steps, with one local commit after each step and no push

1. **Save the prediction.** Create `spe/`. Write `spe/spec/transcripts/2026-10-21-r01.md` with the user's prompt verbatim. Write `spe/spec/spec.md` and `spe/spec/disagreements.md`. Copy this plan to `spe/plans/r01.md`. Write `spe/predictions/r01.yaml` with the header `# Saved before the eval ran. Do not edit after the run.` Commit `spe(r01): spec, plan, and prediction`.
2. **Load the data.** Split the CSV into `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl` and `spe/evals/data/labels.jsonl`, and gitignore both. Gate: exactly 40 rows, every label within the allowed values, no duplicate IDs. Commit the ignore rule and `spe/evals/data/manifest.json`, which holds IDs, hashes, and label counts.
3. **Build the agent.** Create `triage/agent.py`, which reads one ticket on stdin and prints JSON. Create `triage/prompts/definitions.md`, plus `triage/prompts/fewshot.md` for config B. Create `triage/config.py` with the pinned model IDs and the price table. Gate: the R9 hash scan passes. Commit.
4. **Build the grader.** Create `spe/evals/harness/grade.py` with code checks first and the judge second. Create `spe/evals/harness/judge_rubric.md` with 4 items: it addresses the ask, it makes no commitments, it asks for missing info, and its tone fits support. The judge sees the ticket and the reply. It does not see the config name or the reference labels. Commit.
5. **Write the Workflow.** Create `spe/evals/harness/r01-workflow.js` with a single `ROUND = "r01"` constant. Trials receive only ticket text and return the schema. Commit.
6. **Run the gates in order.**
   - Grader selftest: the oracle labels score 1.00, empty output fails, and shuffled labels fail.
   - Control regrade: r01 has no prior round. I log this gate as not applicable.
   - Dry run: 3 cells, which are tickets 1 to 3 on config A, B, and C.

   Commit the gate logs.
7. **Launch the Workflow.** The Workflow returns at launch. I wait for its completion notice.
8. **Close out.** Write `spe/prediction-log.md`, `spe/failures.md`, a "Proposed for round 2" table in `spe/spec/spec.md`, `spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml` with `status: draft`, and `spe/README.md`. Commit and add the local tag `spe-r01`.

### Workflow arguments

| Argument | Value |
|---|---|
| `ROUND` | `"r01"` |
| `configs` | `["A", "B", "C"]` |
| `tickets` | `spe/evals/data/tickets.jsonl` (40 tickets) |
| `repeats` | 3 per ticket per config, so 360 agent trials |
| `split_extra` | Up to 2 more repeats when a ticket's repeats disagree. The cap is 60 extra trials. |
| `judge` | Opus, pinned. One call per trial. |
| `concurrency` | 4 |
| `caps` | 500 agent calls, 500 judge calls, $15 API spend, 60 minutes of wall time. Trials that would cross a cap are skipped and logged. |
| `leak_scan` | Void any trial whose transcript references `labels.jsonl`, `grade.py`, `judge_rubric.md`, or `spe/predictions/` |
| `final_steps` | Failure analysis that groups misses by confusion pair, then a completeness critic |

### Cost estimate (not measured)

- Agent calls use about 0.65M input tokens and 0.11M output tokens.
- Judge calls use about 0.55M input tokens and 0.07M output tokens.
- I expect the total to stay under the $15 cap. I will check this against current list prices in step 3 before launch.

### Halt conditions

The run stops and I report back if any of these happens:
- A cap is hit.
- A trial is found reading the labels.
- The grader selftest fails.
- The CSV does not contain 40 labeled tickets.
critiques: The Requirements (r01) table turns the user's words into R1 to R9. Each row has a Source column that quotes the prompt or names a logged default, and a Test column. Examples are R4, which maps "triage tickets correctly" to category accuracy, and R6, which maps "cheaply" to tokens and USD per ticket.

The Predictions table gives numeric bands for configs A, B, and C on every metric. Examples are category accuracy of 0.85 ± 0.07, 0.88 ± 0.07, and 0.80 ± 0.08, and input tokens of 1300 ± 300 and 2800 ± 500.

Every metric row has a Why column. One example says "Billing and account overlap... Examples help at those boundaries. The smaller model is weaker there." Another gives a token breakdown of about 800 tokens for definitions and about 400 for a ticket. USD is explicitly left unpredicted.

Step 1 copies the plan to spe/plans/r01.md and writes spe/predictions/r01.yaml with a do-not-edit header. It commits both as "spe(r01): spec, plan, and prediction". This happens well before the Workflow launch in step 7.

Step 5 writes r01-workflow.js. Step 6 runs gates in order: a grader selftest with oracle, empty, and shuffled cases, then a control regrade logged as not applicable, then a 3-cell dry run. The full launch comes after these gates.

The Predictions table has a Grader check column for each metric. Examples are jsonschema validation, exact match by majority vote, absolute difference of at most 1, the R8 regex plus a 4-item judge rubric, and API usage.input_tokens.

Step 8 writes spe/prediction-log.md and spe/failures.md. The plan defines a hit as the measured value falling inside the band. Step 8 also seeds the next round with a "Proposed for round 2" table and spe/predictions/r02-draft.yaml with status: draft. The comparison is implied by prediction-log.md and the hit definition rather than spelled out, but it is clear enough to pass.
